chapterName: Early Republic: The Conflict of the Orders - Toward Resolution (450-367 BCE)

briefing.title: Rome, around 390 BC
paragraphs: Rome is a small but ambitious city on the river Tiber, just 16 km from its great Etruscan rival, Veii. At home, a small hereditary aristocracy, the patricians, controls the top offices and the Senate. The plebeian majority, many of them small farmers, are buried in debt and short of land.

Within a few decades Rome will conquer Veii and be humiliated by Gallic warriors who sack the city. Then comes a bitter ten-year political fight at home. At stake: who may rule Rome, and whether ordinary citizens will finally get relief.

timelines.name: The Big Turning Points
timelines.blurb: Four milestones from Rome's struggles at home and abroad.

events.label: Consular tribunes replace the consuls
events.fact: From 444 BC Rome was often run by three to six 'military tribunes with consular power' instead of two consuls.

events.label: Camillus captures Veii
events.fact: Roman troops climbed out of a tunnel inside Juno's temple while Veii's defenders rushed to the walls.

events.label: Senate accepts the tribunes' reforms
events.fact: After ten years of strife, the Senate accepted the whole package of laws pushed by Licinius and Sextius.

events.label: Rome crushes the Senones
events.fact: Even after Rome crushed this Gallic tribe, Roman fear of the Gauls persisted for centuries.

timelines.name: From Gauls to Plebeian Consuls
timelines.blurb: Six steps from a military disaster to shared high office.

events.label: Plebeians dominate consular tribunes
events.fact: After only two plebeians among about a hundred consular tribunes, plebeians made up the majority in some years from around 400 BC.

events.label: Romans routed at the Allia
events.fact: Brennus attacked the Roman reserves on a hill, panic spread, and many Romans drowned in the Tiber.

events.label: Two tribunes launch a ten-year campaign
events.fact: Gaius Licinius Stolo and Lucius Sextius Lateranus put bills on debt, land and the consulship to the Plebeian Council.

events.label: Sextius becomes first plebeian consul
events.fact: Patricians refused to confirm Sextius's election, riots broke out, and the plebeians came close to a mass walkout.

events.label: Law of Genucius shares the consulship
events.fact: The law of the tribune Lucius Genucius apparently required one consul to be a plebeian, and regular sharing began.

events.label: First plebeian praetor elected
events.fact: Plebeians had to wait thirty years after the 366 BC compromise before one of them became praetor, Rome's chief judge.

timelines.name: A Century of Fear and Reform
timelines.blurb: Eight events, from Veii's fall to long-delayed equality.

events.label: Romans tunnel into Veii
events.fact: The Romans dug through the soft volcanic rock beneath Veii after the defenders wrecked their siege equipment.

events.label: Gauls sack Rome
events.fact: According to Livy, the Gauls found the gates open, massacred the old ex-officials and plundered and burned houses.

events.label: Tribunes yield after Velitrae attacks
events.fact: Licinius and Sextius ended their five-year block on elections when Velitrae, a Volscian town, attacked Roman land.

events.label: Senate names Camillus dictator again
events.fact: Camillus threatened violence against the reformers, then resigned for unclear reasons.

events.label: Run of all-patrician consuls begins
events.fact: From 355 to 343 BC both consuls were patricians, showing the 367 BC law did not guarantee sharing.

events.label: Gallic raiders strike near Rome
events.fact: Gallic raiders struck the region around Rome in 350 and again in 349 BC.

events.label: Gauls and Greeks buried alive
events.fact: In 228, 216 and 114 BC Romans buried alive a pair of Gauls and a pair of Greeks, though human sacrifice was not a Roman custom.

events.label: Two plebeians share the consulship
events.fact: Only in 173 BC did two plebeians hold the consulship together for the first time.

matchSets.name: Offices and Terms
matchSets.blurb: Match each Roman term to what it meant.

pairs.name: Consular tribunes
pairs.match: Three to six officials who often replaced the two consuls

pairs.name: Dictator
pairs.match: Emergency commander with sweeping powers for six months

pairs.name: Tribune of the plebs
pairs.match: Plebeian-elected protector who could veto official business

pairs.name: Praetor
pairs.match: Chief judge, first reserved for patricians in 366 BC

pairs.name: Sibylline Books
pairs.match: Prophecies consulted in times of plague, famine or war

trueFalseDecks.name: Veii and the Gauls
trueFalseDecks.blurb: Conquest, catastrophe and the stories told about them.

cards.claim: Veii, the Etruscan city Rome besieged, lay just 16 km from Rome.
cards.why: Veii was a large Etruscan city only 16 km (10 miles) from Rome.

cards.claim: Roman troops emerged from their tunnel inside the temple of Apollo at Veii.
cards.why: They climbed out inside the temple of Juno, Veii's protecting goddess. Apollo was promised a tenth of the spoils.

cards.claim: The Senones, a Gallic tribe, settled on the Adriatic coast around modern Rimini.
cards.why: The Senones were one of several Celtic peoples who had pushed into northern Italy, settling around Rimini.

cards.claim: Rome handed the three Fabius brothers over to the Gauls to avoid war.
cards.why: Instead of handing them over, the Romans elected the brothers consular tribunes for the next year, which enraged the Gauls.

cards.claim: The honking of Juno's sacred geese woke Marcus Manlius during a night attack.
cards.why: While guards and dogs slept, the geese roused Manlius, who hurled the first attacker down the slope.

cards.claim: The Romans agreed to pay the Gauls a ransom of a hundred pounds of gold.
cards.why: Famine and disease forced a deal of a thousand pounds of gold.

cards.claim: The Greek historians Polybius and Diodorus both describe Camillus rescuing Rome.
cards.why: Neither Polybius nor Diodorus mentions Camillus, which is why many historians see his rescue as a later addition.

cards.claim: Rome's huge new wall was built of yellow stone quarried in Veii's territory.
cards.why: The old wall used crumbly local stone; the new 11 km wall used better yellow stone from Veii's land.

trueFalseDecks.name: Plebeians Fight for Power
trueFalseDecks.blurb: Offices, laws and the long road to sharing power.

cards.claim: Livy said the consular tribunate was created as a concession because plebeians could hold it.
cards.why: Livy, writing centuries later, presented the office as a concession open to plebeians.

cards.claim: Between 444 and 401 BC, about half of all consular tribunes were plebeians.
cards.why: Only two of about a hundred consular tribunes in those years were plebeians.

cards.claim: Licinius and Sextius blocked the election of consular tribunes for five years.
cards.why: They struck back at the patricians' vetoes this way, giving in only in 370 BC when Velitrae attacked.

cards.claim: The land law limited any individual to about 3,000 acres of public land.
cards.why: The limit was about 300 acres, and no one could graze more than 100 cattle on public land.

cards.claim: Licinius himself was later fined for breaking his own land limit.
cards.why: Such laws were easy to dodge, and Licinius was later fined for exceeding his own limit.

cards.claim: The new law put ten priests, five of them plebeians, in charge of the Sibylline Books.
cards.why: They replaced the two patrician guardians, breaking the patrician monopoly on priesthoods for the first time.

cards.claim: Under the compromise of 366 BC, the new praetor had to be a plebeian.
cards.why: The nobles accepted a plebeian consul, and in return the plebeians agreed the praetor would be a patrician.

cards.claim: From 355 to 343 BC, one consul each year was always a plebeian.
cards.why: In those years both consuls were patricians; regular sharing began only after Genucius's law of 342 BC.

oddOneOut.why: Three were bills Licinius and Sextius put to the Plebeian Council. The patrician praetorship came later, as Livy's compromise of 366 BC.
Veii, Clusium and Caere are described as Etruscan cities. Ardea is simply a town south of Rome, where Camillus lived in exile.

items: Vowed a tenth of spoils to Apollo
Invited Juno to move to Rome
oddOneOut.why: The first three are what Camillus did to take Veii. His recall from exile at Ardea belongs to Livy's story of the Gallic sack.
Fighting men and senators withdrew to the Capitoline and the Vestals fled to Caere. The old ex-officials stayed outside their houses and were massacred.
Three were roles of the praetor. The Sibylline Books were guarded by priests, first two patricians, later ten.
Livy blames the Allia defeat on three Roman errors. The night attack was the Gauls' later climb up the Capitoline.
The Sibylline Books were consulted in times of plague, famine or war. Elections are not mentioned as an occasion.

whoAmI.name: Faces of the Gallic Crisis
whoAmI.blurb: Romans and Gauls caught up in the fall of Rome.

people.name: Marcus Furius Camillus
clues: Many modern historians think my most famous rescue was added to the story later.
Livy says Rome recalled me from exile at Ardea to be dictator.
I vowed a tenth of the spoils to Apollo and invited Juno to move to Rome.
As dictator, I captured Veii by sending troops through a tunnel.

people.name: Brennus
clues: My warriors struck the Roman reserves on a hill, and panic spread.
I led the Gauls at the battle where many Romans drowned in the Tiber.
When the Romans complained about rigged weights, I threw my sword onto the scales.
I declared, 'Woe to the vanquished!'

people.name: Marcus Manlius
clues: I had once served as consul of Rome.
I was among the defenders on the Capitoline, Rome's citadel hill, during the siege.
One night I was roused while the guards and dogs slept.
Woken by Juno's honking geese, I hurled the first Gallic climber down the slope.

people.name: Lucius Albinus
clues: Aristotle's 'certain Lucius' who saved Rome might have been me.
I was no magistrate, just a citizen passing by as Rome emptied.
I carried sacred objects to Caere, an allied Etruscan city on the coast.
I gave the Vestal Virgins a lift on my wagon.
reviewFlags: a clue contains the person’s name

whoAmI.name: Who Told the Story?
whoAmI.blurb: Ancient and modern writers who shaped how we see these events.

people.name: Livy
clues: I claimed Rome's tangled streets came from hasty rebuilding after the Gauls burned it.
I called some tribunes 'slaves of the nobility'.
I wrote that the patricians and plebeians were 'at length brought into harmony'.
I am the Roman historian in whose story Camillus arrives just in time to cancel the ransom.

people.name: Diodorus Siculus
clues: Like Polybius, I never mention Camillus in the story of the sack.
In my account, the Gauls had gone on to southern Italy before they were beaten.
I was a Greek historian writing about Rome's past.
I say an Etruscan army defeated the Gauls on their way back from southern Italy.

people.name: T. J. Cornell
clues: I think the Gauls left most of Rome standing and went home once paid.
I doubt the tale of Aruns's revenge and suspect the Senones were mercenaries.
I argue the new plebeian leaders joined the patricians in a new aristocracy.
I am a modern historian who trusts very little of Livy's dramatic story.

places.name: Veii
places.why: Rome's great Etruscan rival, captured by Camillus through a tunnel around 396 BC.

places.name: Clusium
places.why: The Etruscan town, now Chiusi, whose appeal to Rome against the Senones led to the Gallic war.

places.name: Caere
places.why: Rome's coastal Etruscan ally, where the Vestal Virgins took the sacred objects during the sack.

places.name: Ardea
places.why: The town south of Rome where, according to Livy, Camillus was living in exile when recalled as dictator.
reviewFlags: no coordinates on Wikipedia "Ardea, Lazio"; position is the model's estimate

places.name: Velitrae
places.why: The Volscian town whose attack in 370 BC made Licinius and Sextius end their block on elections.

places.name: Cumae
places.why: The Greek city near Naples where, by tradition, King Tarquinius Superbus bought the Sibylline Books.

places.name: Rimini
places.why: The Adriatic coast around modern Rimini was where the Senones, the Gauls who sacked Rome, had settled.
